content: Walter Walt Dawson, born on April 26, 1982, in Portland, Oregon, is a prominent advocate for Alzheimer's disease. He is the son of Cecil Dawson, a British immigrant, and Clara Dawson, a native of Oregon. As a young boy, Dawson gained national attention by initiating a letter-writing campaign to advocate for his father and others affected by Alzheimer's disease. This campaign highlighted the challenges faced by families dealing with the condition. In 1992, Dawson became a national spokesperson for the Alzheimer's Association. He was invited multiple times to testify before committees in the United States Senate and House of Representatives, sharing his family's experiences with the disease. During his time in Washington, Dawson had the opportunity to meet with senior legislators and public officials, including President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore. Dawson's letter-writing campaign began as a response to the financial strain his family faced due to the high cost of his father’s long-term care. National Public Radio (NPR) was the first major media outlet to support his campaign, featuring him reading one of his letters on air when he was just nine years old. Following this, major networks such as NBC, CBS, and Nickelodeon covered his story, bringing widespread attention to the struggles of Alzheimer's patients and their families. These media appearances helped raise awareness about the need for healthcare reform and the challenges associated with Alzheimer's disease. As he transitioned into adulthood, Dawson continued his advocacy work, focusing on addressing issues related to Alzheimer's disease and promoting healthcare reform. While pursuing his undergraduate studies at the University of Portland, he was elected Student Body Vice-President and served as President of the Student Senate. After completing his undergraduate degree, Dawson spent a year with AmeriCorps before moving to England to study at the London School of Economics. In the fall of 2007, he began a postgraduate degree in Comparative Health Policy at Oxford University, furthering his commitment to improving healthcare systems and policies.
